messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 35-year-old Vietnamese American physical therapist who presented for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of intimate partner violence perpetrated by her former husband. Married at 28, Linh described a relationship that deteriorated steadily over four years, culminating in repeated episodes of physical assault. The most severe incident occurred on a winter evening when her husband, after forcing her to remain in the kitchen while he berated her — gripping her wrists so she could not leave — pressed her bare arms against a cold window pane and struck her across the face and shoulders. She recalled the sensation of the cold glass against her skin with terrible precision. It is that specificity — the cold, the grip, the absolute inability to move — that has made ordinary life feel like a minefield ever since.

Linh left the relationship approximately fourteen months ago and relocated with the help of her sister. In the months that followed, she began noticing that certain sensory experiences seemed to reach back through time and pull her directly into that kitchen. The cold of an examination table in her clinic, the brush of a patient's hand repositioning during a session, or a moment in which a supervisor directed her to perform a procedure in a specific way — any of these could detonate without warning. When they did, the memory did not feel like a memory. Linh described it as suddenly being back there, not recalling but reliving, with no felt sense that it was over and she was safe. The overwhelm that accompanied these intrusions was so total that she had, on several occasions, had to excuse herself from a treatment room mid-session, unable to complete her explanation of what had happened to her patient or to herself.

These intrusive episodes fed directly into a set of beliefs about herself that had been hardening since the abuse began. When the memory returned with its full sensory force, Linh found herself arriving at the same conclusions: that she had provoked it, that she had stayed too long, that a woman without some fundamental defect would not have found herself in that position. She had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that the event had happened because of the way she had acted, and that something was broken in her at a level that could not be repaired. The humiliation she carried was not merely situational; it felt constitutional — a permanent mark others could see even when she smiled.

These appraisals, in turn, shaped how she moved through her days. Certain that she was defective and blameworthy, Linh found herself scanning every clinical interaction for signs that a patient or colleague might become threatening, reading neutral facial expressions as harbingers of aggression. This hypervigilance kept her body in a state of constant readiness, which meant that ordinary tactile contact — unavoidable in her work as a physical therapist — registered as threat rather than routine, and the cycle of intrusion would begin again. She also spent hours replaying the relationship, asking what she could have done differently, and grieving the version of herself she remembered from before: someone lighter, more trusting, less afraid. This dwelling neither resolved the questions nor quieted the grief; it only kept the material vivid and close, so that the next cold surface or unexpected touch arrived in already-primed nervous system.

The consequences accumulated in ways that were both relational and professional. Linh had quietly reduced the number of hands-on techniques she offered patients, rerouting to verbal instruction wherever possible, and her caseload had narrowed. Her husband — now a new partner she described as gentle and patient — had noticed her flinching and her silences, and she had been unable to explain clearly what was happening when he asked; she would begin and lose the thread, the words dissolving under the weight of what she was trying to carry.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a moment three weeks prior when a patient, a large man, had placed his hand on her forearm to steady himself, and she had frozen entirely, dissociated in the middle of the clinic floor. She is most afraid, she said quietly at the end of the intake, that this is simply who she is now. What she hopes, though she can barely articulate it, is that it is not.
